briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Relief on the Horizon: MI Operators Adapt as Both Governor Candidates Target the 24% Tax — Nationally, DEA and FDA Keep Pushing Forward
briefs.top: Michigan operators are finding workarounds to the wholesale tax squeeze — from supplier cost-sharing to settled regulatory disputes — while both major-party candidates for governor are now on record vowing to roll it back. Nationally, the DEA's rescheduling review keeps clearing procedural checkpoints and the FDA is barreling toward a landmark September 14 psychedelics hearing, with Compass Pathways and the VA both racing toward real-world psilocybin therapy.

local.text: Upper Peninsula chain Rize is proving the tax doesn't have to be fatal to growth: the three-location operator has kept expanding by negotiating cost-sharing deals with suppliers instead of eating the 24% hit alone — a playbook other operators can copy.

Jars Cannabis notched a win in Madison Heights, reaching a deal with the city to remove a Flock surveillance camera aimed at its parking lot after mounting a sign to block its view — the camera came down pending council approval, easing a years-long compliance headache for the 54-store chain.

Tax-relief momentum is now bipartisan at the top of the ticket: GOP gubernatorial nominee John James pledged August 19 to repeal or sharply cut the 24% wholesale tax, joining Democratic hopeful Chris Swanson, who has already vowed to "work to roll back the 24 percent wholesale excise tax." With both parties' standard-bearers publicly committed, operators have real leverage heading into 2026.

Demand hasn't collapsed — it's just moved: statewide flower inventory at retail is up 58% year-over-year and processor stock is up 140%, and with prices still near all-time lows, retailers, not wholesalers, are holding the pricing power in this market.

The hard number to watch: Higher Love, a U.P. dispensary chain, closed five of its nine locations, with its president attributing the closures entirely to the tax — a reminder of why the bipartisan repeal push above matters so much for the back half of the year.

national.text: The DEA's cannabis rescheduling review cleared a key procedural milestone on August 18, keeping the multi-year push to move cannabis to Schedule III alive and on track — a shift that would preserve federal prohibition while easing the 280E tax burden that currently hammers operators.

The FDA is set to hold its landmark public hearing on the therapeutic future of psychedelics on September 14 in a hybrid format at its White Oak campus, following the agency's release of final clinical trial guidance covering psilocybin, LSD and MDMA — the clearest regulatory roadmap this drug class has ever gotten.

The Department of Veterans Affairs officially launched PIVOT on August 5, a five-site clinical trial evaluating psilocybin for veterans with treatment-resistant depression, running on Compass Pathways' donated COMP360 formulation — a major real-world validation for the leading psilocybin drug candidate.

Compass Pathways is completing a rolling New Drug Application for COMP360 after the drug showed six-month durability in treatment-resistant depression, with final submission on track for Q4 2026 and a possible U.S. launch in the first half of 2027.

Consolidation capital is flowing back in: Holistic Industries picked up Cannabist's Ohio operations for $47M and British American Tobacco announced an investment in Charlotte's Web, a signal that big tobacco capital is circling branded cannabis as rescheduling optimism builds deal activity.
